Sorry if the formatting here is a bit rambling. I just watched it and tossed in the occasional note here while doing so.

In general I have mixed feelings about it. On the plus side, I really do like that it treats the weight issue as a serious problem. I also like that it pointed out how much work needs to go into burning off food. I think it's far too common for people to think that light exercise every few days means they can eat like a pig. But there is some bad to that which I'll hit later.

They also did a good job giving an overview of some of the history of America's relation to health, food and obesity.

I mostly liked the promotion of "real food" that actually has some resemblance to what you'd find in nature.

On the negative side...there's a lot of negatives.

I think it's always a good idea to pause documentaries at the beginning and check on the background of the people chosen to be the first voices of authority. You can usually get a good idea of how things are going to proceed from there. With Fed Up one of the first people is a pop-science reporter with no accademic background in medicine or biology talking about how it's impossible to stay thin by counting calories unless you're a "guiness book of world records" level counter.

I thought it was telling that the first guy to state that type of food is more important than calories is, looking at his neck and face, skinnyfat.

They used a lot of "we're not sayin', but we're just saaayyyyin is all....." type of suggestion a lot. Interest in fitness came about at the same time as an increase in obesity? Well obviously it must mean that people just suddenly thought that light aroebics meant they could finally eat those cakes they'd previously been avoiding! And also in the "we're just sayin'...." category would be SPOOOOOKKKKYYYY MUSIC to tell us who bad guys are.

There's a fair amount of the worst kind of emotional manipulation in documentaries. Where scenes are edited to show the "bad guys" stumbling over words or adjusting ties. It's a cheap tactic that never speaks well of a documentary. Having good and bad guys in a documentary is in itself usually not the best sign of media that's documenting events rather than creating the story someone wants to tell.

The "sugar is more addictive than cocaine" thing, ugh.

All of the pleas to think of the children. Is that an issue, of course it is. But it's also one of the best ways to manipulate an audience. It brings along a side benefit of audience members who might be uncomfortable with their own weight being able to think that it's better to focus on the next generation rather than their own lifestyle.

I really disliked how exercise was treated. It often felt like they were portraying it as some kind of magic weight loss pill which just wasn't working. And from a pure calorie to calorie ratio I'd agree it's not the best thing in the world for losing weight. But it is the best for being healthy. But more importantly when it comes to fat people, it's time and entertainment that doesn't involve easy snacking.

There were also a few things that I had mixed feelings on. The big topic, sugar, is the most significant. Bringing it up as an issue was good. Showing the politics behind having a sugar rda was good. Making it the answer to the very complex question of obesity in America was bad.

I think were intentionally misleading when talking about school lunches in order to make it a more interesting story. I never bought lunches in high school, and that seemed to be the norm from what I saw. Anecdote and all, I know. But looking it up it seems that only around 44% of high school kids get their lunch from the school. Fed Up never outright stated anything to the contrary there. But it felt like they were intentionally sugesting that most kids were getting school lunches. To the point where I had to pause and check to see if there was some new policy implemented to make it mandatory since I was in school.

To go back to what I liked about promoting "real food", I also disliked the larger message it was a part of. If the food subreddit has taught me anything it's that a determined fatty can turn even the healthiest thing into an abomination. Or another example, the soggy dressing dripping salads dieting fatties love so much.

They did a good job laying out a theory for why people are getting so fat. They didn't do a very good job applying it to the existing data though. I would have liked to see the documentary touch on why gender, ethnic background and socioeconomic status influence it. And why the stats there can be flipped between different countries. To be a bit more blunt, I'd like the slim rich people on camera to talk about why they feel they're personally immune to a lot of the influence and advertising while other people aren't. I'll admit that's a bit unfair of me but it often felt like the elephant in the room. Why do you feel you're able to make the rational choice with food while other people need to be tricked or forced into it? I get that it might be beyond the scope of the documentary. But I think it would have really added to the discussion to bring in people to talk about teaching critical thinking skills in school, how to deconstruct advertising in media, possibly even structuring events to promote the development of more mature self-control. And that's generally my biggest problem with the documentary. It's trying to provide a simple answer to a very complex question. And often without properly looking into the assumptions the people behind it have brought with them.

Other than that there isn't much to say, they are pretty durable so some scuffs and scratches are pretty normal for a functioning system.

I've been having a very difficult time fighting this boss, I always die within the first phase and can't get close to him. Anyone have any tips?
This is the boss with the laser barriers on the sides right? My goto strategy was to use the level 1/2 knife and stay on one of the platforms. It worked for me to also cut down incoming projectiles.

The Blade is essentially made just for this boss. Depending on whether you want fast damage, or to remove the projectiles Monster X makes, you should be using Level 2 Blade or Level 3 Blade, respectively. You should try and get rid of the beetles in the arena first - they can be huge pains, especially in Phase 2. Remember that Monster X will always charge towards you - so if you stand on his left left, he will charge to the left, and vice versa. You can easily jump between the legs, too, so don't be afraid to get close to the edge of the arena.
